text: People own graphs: one-click graph on a host, links between graphs, one global graph across servers
description:
Felix 2026-11-12: "that actually comes closest to the reality: People owning graphs. Everyone can make a proposal which is his graph. And then ideally the website would be able to access different servers (almost like federated)." The hurdle to participate is too high today: you have to set up a repo. "If we could make that simple and one-click, that'd be awesome. Then the result would really be a global ever expanding graph of ideas. aimparency. ideaparency. global. I'd love this."

What led here (2026-11-11): every design that put all people into one graph needed rules for who may touch which idea (owners and levels per idea, signed commits, a GitHub check, a guest layer) and felt cumbersome or like a compromise. Here the unit of ownership is the graph: whoever owns a graph may change all of it.

Fits the standing decision of 2026-06-27 and 2026-09-20 (e81b11c3): links are to a whole graph, which stays a black box.

Exists today: an idea supported by a whole linked repo, drawn as one node with value flow (e81b11c3); opening any graph from a Git URL read-only in the normal UI, with a shareable link (250fb1aa, 9beb3725); spinning a branch off into its own graph (10a0561b); hosted mode with accounts for one project per server (af701cd6).

Missing, not designed: a host that holds many graphs, each with its own address; creating a graph there in one click, without a repo; linking to a graph by address instead of a local checkout; the offer side of a link (a graph says which idea of another graph it supports, with a pitch) and its acceptance; the website opening a graph that lives on another server.

status.comment: Direction Felix says he would love (2026-11-12); not designed, nothing built, no build requested. If it holds, owners and levels per idea (fcb38df6), the guest layer (34b3d747) and the GitHub check (698badcb) are probably not needed.
